moments.title: “A crooked tree lives its own life, but a straight tree is turned into wood.” - Chinese Proverb The idea behind this proverb comes most clearly from the writings of Zhuangzi, one of the central thinkers of Daoism in the
moments.selftext: “A crooked tree lives its own life, but a straight tree is turned into wood.” - Chinese Proverb The idea behind this proverb comes most clearly from the writings of Zhuangzi, one of the central thinkers of Daoism in the 4th century BCE. In the Zhuangzi, a famous story tells of a large, twisted tree that carpenters ignore because its wood is unsuitable for construction. Precisely because it is considered “useless,” the tree is never cut down and survives to live out its natural life. Zhuangzi uses the tree as a metaphor for human life. In Daoist thought, being “useful” by conventional standards can make a person vulnerable to exploitation, control, and exhaustion. Those who are unconventional, overlooked, or unwilling to fit society’s expectations may instead preserve their freedom and live on their own terms.

moments.selftext: Absolutely insane. This might be the clearest glimpse yet of how AI will transform scientific discovery. Anthropic asked an unreleased version of Claude to take a real stab at the Riemann Hypothesis, one of the most famous unsolved problems in mathematics. It failed. But while failing, Claude unexpectedly improved a longstanding lower bound for the proportion of zeros of the Riemann zeta function known to satisfy the hypothesis, from 41.6% to 67.2%. Claude coordinated 60 subagents, tested hundreds of ideas, searched the literature, challenged its own proof, and formalized the result in Lean. This is what the beginning of autonomous AI-driven scientific discovery looks like. Unironically, the Rienann hypothesis will probably be solved in the very near future. I am speechless.

moments.selftext: Florence Pugh during Season 7 of Running Wild with Bear Grylls, as she spent two days navigating the rugged Costa Rican rainforest alongside Bear Grylls. Florence Pugh traded movie sets for the Costa Rican rainforest when she joined Bear Grylls on Running Wild. Over two days, she rappelled from a helicopter, crossed rushing rivers, climbed through waterfalls and cliffs, and learned survival skills she eventually had to put into practice herself to reach their extraction point. It offered fans a completely different look at Pugh beyond the characters she plays on screen.
